articles.title: Eye on Everything
articles.summary: This article details upcoming events for the SJAA, including June, July, and August meetings featuring member presentations, lunar nomenclature, and a talk on Kitt Peak. It also announces July star parties at Yosemite, an August star-b-q at Fremont Peak, and a call for volunteers for the observatory committee which has $6,000 for building. Additionally, it notes Crazy Ed's as the new US distributor for the Herald-Bobroff AstroAtlas.

articles.title: Activities Calendar
articles.summary: This document outlines the activities calendar for June and July, primarily featuring general meetings, board meetings, and various star parties at locations like Houge Park, Henry Coe, Fremont Peak, Grant Ranch, and Yosemite. It also includes Observational Astronomy classes and notes specific astronomical events like the summer solstice and moon phases. Key topics for general meetings include equipment discussions, new by-law votes, and lectures on lunar nomenclature.

articles.title: Extra, Extra!! Read All About It!! Bits of Lunar Crater Fall to Earth!!
articles.summary: This article discusses Dean R. Chapman's controversial 1967 theory proposing that certain tektites found on Earth, particularly across Southeast Asia to Northwest Australia, are actually ejecta from the Moon's Tycho crater. Chapman's hypothesis challenges the conventional terrestrial origin of tektites, suggesting they were formed during a single lunar impact event about 700,000 years ago and exhibiting patterns consistent with moon-to-Earth trajectories. Despite mathematical models supporting the idea that 100 million tons of this lunar material fell to Earth, the theory has not been universally accepted by scientists.

articles.title: Tektites, continued from page 1
articles.summary: The article explores the hypothesis that tektites are lunar ejecta, specifically correlating their global distribution with trajectories from the Moon's Tycho crater. It speculates that this theory might have influenced the original plans for Apollo 17's landing site near Tycho, prompting the author to playfully assert the lunar origin of his own tektites, referencing Chapman's scientific work.

articles.title: Obsession 15" First Light by Rich Neuschaefer
articles.summary: Rich Neuschaefer describes the "first light" experience with his new Obsession 15" f4.5 truss tube Dobsonian telescope at Fremont Peak State Park. Despite bright skies, he praises the scope's excellent design, easy assembly, smooth operation, and superior optical performance, noting sharp views of stars, Jupiter, M13, and other galaxies. The article highlights the enjoyment and quality of his initial extended observing session.

articles.title: Fight Light Pollution: Join the I.D.A. by John Dellinges
articles.summary: Light pollution is a significant problem for amateur astronomers, degrading the night sky and necessitating travel to dark sites. The article urges stargazers to join the International Dark Sky Association (IDA), a non-profit organization dedicated to combating light pollution, highlighting that increased membership strengthens their advocacy. By joining for $20 a year, members support the fight against light pollution and gain access to resources and meetings, ultimately helping to preserve dark skies for current and future generations.

articles.title: Observing Report, Fremont Peak, May 11, 1996
articles.summary: This observing report details a star party held at Fremont Peak on May 11, 1996, where initial cloudiness cleared for a night of astronomy. Despite low-level haze and light pollution from San Jose, observers enjoyed steady, transparent skies and viewed various deep-sky objects, a detailed Jupiter, and a promising Comet Hale-Bopp through numerous telescopes. The event was described as the first summer-like star party of the year, bringing together many amateur astronomers.

articles.title: Eyepiece Types
articles.summary: Jim Van Nuland discusses his personal eyepiece preferences and experiences, primarily using Meade "Research-Grade" Abbe Orthoscopics and an Erfle for his 8-inch f/6 Newtonian. He advocates for a closely-spaced series of magnifications to optimize contrast and field size for deep-sky objects and planets, while also highly recommending a 28mm Pretoria for fast rich-field telescopes. Van Nuland emphasizes that eyepiece selection is highly personal, influenced by factors like telescope type, observer's age, and eye pupil size, advising beginners to try before they buy.

articles.title: Periodical Publication Statement
articles.summary: The document is a periodical publication statement for the SJAA Ephemeris, the newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association. It states that the newsletter is published monthly, 12 times a year, from January through December. The association's mailing address is also provided.

articles.title: Houge Park Status Report
articles.summary: Jim Van Nuland's May 7th visit to Houge Park detailed progress on the tennis courts, including a newly painted fence, laid sod, and tree planting. A temporary fence will remain around the grass for about a month to allow it to establish. Consequently, the basketball court may still be needed for upcoming star parties.

articles.title: Swap Meet and Auction Results
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) held a successful Swap Meet and Auction, generating a total of $793.50 from raffle, auction bidder fees/commissions, and swap meet sales. The event also resulted in the addition of five new members to the SJAA. The article concludes that it was a very good day for the organization.

articles.title: The Probe Story: Secrets and Surprises from Jupiter
articles.summary: The Galileo Probe's initial data from Jupiter, presented in January 1996, revealed a generally expected but surprisingly detailed picture of the planet's atmosphere. Key findings included a new, powerful radiation belt, a denser and hotter upper atmosphere, unexpected cloud compositions (or lack thereof), a much drier atmosphere than predicted, and higher concentrations of certain noble gases, prompting a significant rethinking of Jupiter's origin and structure. The probe's entry into a 'hot spot' also highlighted the planet's atmospheric heterogeneity.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: Don Machholz provides an update on comet observations. Comets Hale-Bopp and Kopff are currently visible together in the southern morning Milky Way, accessible with binoculars. Additionally, Comet Schwassmann-Wachmann 1 recently experienced a significant outburst, brightening to magnitude 11, and can be seen in the evening sky south of Regulus.

articles.title: C/1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp)
articles.summary: This document provides ephemeris data for three comets: C/1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp), 22P/Kopff, and 29P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 1. It lists their Right Ascension, Declination, elongation from the Sun, and estimated visual magnitudes for specific dates between late May and early July. This information serves as a guide for observers to locate these comets.

articles.title: Orbital Elements
articles.summary: This document presents a table detailing the orbital elements for three comets: Hale-Bopp, Kopff, and Schwassmann-Wachmann 1. It includes specific astronomical data such as perihelion date and distance, argument of perihelion, ascending node, inclination, eccentricity, and orbital period for each object, along with their respective data sources from Minor Planet Circulars.

articles.title: Lunar time date rise trans set
articles.summary: This document provides a schedule for the major lunar phases, specifically Full Moon, Last Quarter, New Moon, and First Quarter. For each phase, it lists the exact time in PDT, along with the corresponding day, moonrise, moon transit, and moonset times. This information is valuable for planning observations or understanding the moon's position throughout its cycle.

articles.title: Mercury
articles.summary: This document provides astronomical data for the planet Mercury, detailing its distance from Earth and apparent magnitude. It includes an ephemeris table with rise, transit, and set times, along with Right Ascension and Declination for three specific dates.

articles.title: Venus
articles.summary: This article provides an astronomical ephemeris for the planet Venus, detailing its observable characteristics and positional data for three specific dates. It includes Venus's distance from Earth, apparent magnitude, rise, transit, and set times, along with its celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination).

articles.title: Mars
articles.summary: This document presents an astronomical ephemeris for the planet Mars, detailing its current distance (2.34 AU) and magnitude (+1.2). It provides daily observational data for the 7th, 17th, and 27th, including rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination.

articles.title: Jupiter
articles.summary: This document provides current observational data for Jupiter, including its distance and magnitude. It lists ephemeris data for three dates (7th, 17th, 27th), detailing rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination for each period. This information is crucial for planning observations of the gas giant.

articles.title: Saturn
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for Saturn, detailing its distance, magnitude, rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination for three specific dates (7th, 17th, and 27th) within a month. It serves as a guide for observers interested in locating and tracking the planet.

articles.title: SOL Star Type G2V Intelligent Life in System?
articles.summary: The document presents a title questioning the existence of intelligent life within the SOL (Sun) G2V star system. However, the accompanying content consists solely of a table providing astronomical ephemeris data, including rise, transit, and set times, along with Right Ascension and Declination coordinates for several dates. The provided data is observational tracking information for a celestial body, not an analysis of extraterrestrial intelligence.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight
articles.summary: This document presents a table detailing the start and end times of astronomical twilight for several specific Julian Dates in June. It provides precise timeframes when the sky is sufficiently dark for astronomical observations.

articles.title: Sidreal Time
articles.summary: This document presents a table illustrating sidereal time calculations for 'Transit Right Ascension at Local Midnight' on specific dates. It shows the resulting sidereal times on the 7th, 17th, and 27th of an unspecified month as 15:56, 16:34, and 17:14 respectively.

articles.title: Darkest Saturday Night: June 15
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for June 15, detailing key times such as sunset (20:33), twilight end (22:28), moon rise (05:43), and dawn begin (03:49). Originating from the SJAA Ephemeris Page 6, June 1996, it serves as a guide for observing conditions on that specific night.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Status
articles.summary: This document, titled "Telescope Loaner Status" by Paul Barton, provides a detailed list of telescopes available through a loaner program. It itemizes each telescope by description, indicates its current borrower, and specifies the due date, noting which telescopes are currently available for loan. The table serves as a status report for the loaner inventory, showing equipment currently out and when it is expected to be returned.

articles.title: Astro Ads
articles.summary: The "Astro Ads" section features several classified listings for used astronomical equipment, including Dobsonian telescopes from Meade and Orion, and an Astro-Physics APO refractor. Each listing provides a description, price, and contact information, and the service is offered free to noncommercial advertisers.

articles.title: Probe, continued from page 5
articles.summary: This article details the findings and ultimate fate of a probe during its descent into Jupiter's atmosphere. It revealed unexpectedly fast, deep winds driven by internal heat, and a turbulent, dry atmosphere with higher-than-anticipated upper-layer temperatures. Most instruments failed due to extreme conditions, but the atmospheric structure instrument continued transmitting data for 57.6 minutes before the probe succumbed to immense pressure and heat, melting and vaporizing to become part of Jupiter.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors, providing their names, positions (President, VP, Treasurer, Secretary, Director), and associated phone numbers. It serves as a directory for the organization's leadership.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is a membership form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing fees for regular and junior memberships, with an optional add-on for a Sky and Telescope subscription. It provides instructions for submission, including the treasurer's contact information and address, and specifies that checks should be made payable to "SJAA". The form also includes sections for personal contact details and indicates the organization is a non-profit.
